claims.text: The scoped nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios.
The nanoparticles initially exhibit a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by the balance between kinetically limited nanoconfined diffusion and thermodynamically driven segregation.
At lower temperatures, high kinetic barriers inhibit atomic rearrangement.
Inhibited atomic rearrangement at lower temperatures preserves the uniform solid solution.
Increasing temperature sufficiently enhances atomic mobility and nanoconfined diffusion.
Once a critical temperature is exceeded, mixing-enthalpy differences and strain drive local elemental segregation.
Reactive atmospheres promote segregation and surface reconstruction relative to inert atmospheres.
High-temperature diffusion-driven segregation can initiate phase separation or surface reconstruction.
The controlled experiment ramps temperature from 473 K to 1923 K under inert and reactive atmospheres.
Under inert conditions at lower temperatures, the initial single-phase solid-solution structure will be retained.
At higher temperatures, particularly under reactive atmospheres, secondary phases will emerge.
High-temperature instability will produce XRD peak splitting or broadening relative to the initial state.
High-temperature instability will produce elemental clustering detectable by TEM/EDS relative to the initial state.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to nanoparticles having controlled size and morphology and synthesized as uniform solid solutions.
Significant composition imbalance or growth conditions that promote phase separation may cause deviations from the prediction.
The critical temperature and the quantitative effects of particular reactive gases are not specified and remain uncertain.
Retention of a homogeneous single phase near 1923 K under reactive conditions, without statistically significant phase or compositional changes, is designated as the falsifying outcome.
